source.authors: Márlon César Pereira, Ingrid de Carvalho Guimarães, Daniel Acosta-Avalos, William Fernando Antonialli Junior
source.title: Can altered magnetic field affect the foraging behaviour of ants?

method: behavioural: Y-maze choice with Helmholtz coils at one end, coils on versus off
conditions: Wild-collected workers from laboratory colonies (Ectatomma brunneum, 4 colonies, Dourados, Mato Grosso do Sul; Neoponera inversa, 6 colonies, Ilhéus, Bahia), kept in plaster nests at about 22 C. Y-maze 65 cm long, 2.5 cm in diameter, a food resource at each end; Helmholtz coils at one end, 7.5 cm from the resource, raised the horizontal field component to 60 uT (local horizontal 19.8, vertical -10.6, total 22.5 uT), giving a total field of about 60.9 uT, roughly three times local; the direction of the applied field relative to the geomagnetic field is not stated. Control: the same arrangement with the coils switched off. The paper reports 10 foragers per colony, two workers entering the maze at a time, so roughly 40 and 60 workers; trials per condition, order of coils-on and coils-off, and assignment of the coil side are not reported. Chi-square test with the path chosen as the variable, coils on versus off; no choice counts or percentages are printed for either condition. Two ants entered the maze together, so choices may not be independent; whether workers were marked, reused or tested in both conditions, and whether the same colonies served both conditions, is not stated (the maze was cleaned with alcohol between ants). With the coils on, workers chose the path to the resource that was not placed between the activated coils significantly more often; the Results state that no significant difference in decision-making was found when the coils were off. The field is a large change (about three times local), not a threshold; heat from the coils is not excluded: the Discussion says separate tests found ant body heat did not rise significantly with the coils on, but those results are not part of the study, and the authors write that they cannot rule out stress caused by the coils. There were no sham (current-cancelling) coils, so the applied field is not separated from heat or other effects of powering the coils. Ants also stopped moving in 85% (E. brunneum) and 75% (N. inversa) of cases under the applied field. Sample sizes small and the field-inclination values are described inconsistently across sections. The quote reports both species; this line carries Ectatomma brunneum.

source.authors: Xiaoyun Ren, Shengyong Wu, Zhenlong Xing, Ruirui Xu, Wanzhi Cai, Zhongren Lei
source.title: Behavioral Responses of Western Flower Thrips (Frankliniella occidentalis) to Visual and Olfactory Cues at Short Distances

method: behavioural: Y-tube olfactometer, odour source versus hexane control
conditions: Thrips collected from Capsicum annuum in Beijing and reared on Phaseolus vulgaris pods at 26 C, so laboratory-reared stock; females 24 h old, starved 4 h. Y-tube 1 cm inner diameter, 10 cm arms, charcoal-filtered humidified air at 300 mL/min per arm. 60 females tested individually per pairing, observed 5 min, insects making no choice within 3 min discarded; chi-square test against 50:50 (SAS 9.2). The text gives no choice percentages or chi-square values for these two pairings, and does not say whether arms were swapped or the stimulus side randomised. The Y-tube doses are not stated: 10% p-anisaldehyde in hexane is given only for the cylinder assay, and 10 uL of the alfalfa extract only for the card-plus-volatiles cue; the number of thrips recorded as no response is not reported. In the other pairings of the same experiment, a yellow flower-shaped card against black card drew 63.3% (p < 0.001), the card plus volatiles against its control 75.0% against 16.6% (p < 0.001), and the card plus volatiles against the card alone was not significant (55.0% against 30.0%, p = 0.069); the percentages for that pairing sum to 85%, unexplained. Card plus volatiles was chosen over volatiles alone (65.0% against 25.0%, p = 0.001); in the card-versus-volatiles pairing no choice percentages are given, but residence time was longer on the volatiles (213.2 +/- 13.9 s against 177.1 +/- 10.9 s, t47 = 2.59, p = 0.013). Generations in culture not stated; laboratory culture of field-collected stock accepted at species rank (audit 332). Volatile source was flowering alfalfa extract, not the thrips' crop host.
quote: Both PA and plant volatiles extracted from flowering M. sativa had attracting effects on WFT (experiment sets 1 and 2, p = 0.022/0.014), and the extracted volatiles were used as the olfactory cue (O).

source.authors: Kristine Cerbule, Bent Herrmann, Eduardo Grimaldo, Leif Grimsmo, Jørgen Vollstad
source.title: The effect of white and green LED-lights on the catch efficiency of the Barents Sea snow crab (Chionoecetes opilio) pot fishery

method: field experiment: commercial baited pots with and without LED lights on longlines, catch comparison with double-bootstrap confidence intervals
conditions: Wild snow crabs fished commercially in the Barents Sea (ICES 1.b), 250 to 280 m, May 2020; every pot baited with about 800 g squid, pots about 30 m apart. Each longline alternated lit test pots with unlit baseline pots (one test pot after every second or third baseline pot); the alternation was fixed, not randomised. Three series fished on separate longlines: white LED with 8-day soak, white LED with 14-day soak (174 pots across these two) and green LED with 17-day soak (135 pots), each with 48 to 54 test and 81 to 126 baseline pots; 1583 test and 2065 baseline crabs measured in all. Soak time, line and fishing area therefore differ between colours and the paper reports no wavelength, intensity or flashing/constant mode for the PotLight LEDs, and the authors write that the light intensity that can attract the crabs to the pots is unknown, so the stimulus is defined only as white or green light against none and colours are not compared at matched intensity; the three series were not fished simultaneously, and the authors say similar soak times could not be kept. Undersized retention was about 10% in test and 20% in baseline pots in the green series. Catch in a baited pot is a capture outcome (attraction, entry and retention are not separated). White LED legal-size catch rose 52.96% (8 days) and about 52% (14 days); green and white overlapped in confidence intervals, so no colour difference was shown; size-distribution comparisons showed no clear significant differences in any series; undersized retention did not differ significantly from baseline in the green series. The paper reports confidence intervals, not p values, for the catch effects.
quote: In the third series using green LED lights and 17-day soaking time, the catch efficiency of the pots for snow crabs with CW above the minimum landing size increased significantly by 76% (CRaverage+ = 176.38 (CI:145.72–216.07)).

source.authors: Elisabeth H. Koschier, Lena Dittmann, Bernhard Spangl
source.title: Olfactory Responses of Asproparthenis punctiventris Germar to Leaf Odours of Amaranthaceae Plants

method: behavioural: four-arm olfactometer, plant leaf odour against three clean-air arms
conditions: Adults collected in April and May 2021 and 2022 shortly after emergence from overwintering sites in winter wheat fields in the Tullnerfeld region of Lower Austria, with Grandlure-baited pitfall traps; held at 5 C in darkness over winter, unmated, sexes separated 48 to 72 h before testing. Four-arm air-flow olfactometer (30 x 30 x 3.2 cm), 250 mL/min per arm, dark room with a halogen lamp; leaves of young plants (BBCH 14 to 19) harvested about 1 h before each test, three arms carried water-only jars as clean-air control; observation up to 6 min, beetles not leaving the start zone within 3 min excluded. The odour quadrant was always quadrant 1; olfactometer and jars were rotated 90 degrees after every third observation. n = 36 beetles per sex per plant species (12 observations replicated three times). First choices tested by chi-square goodness of fit (df 3), time and visits by Friedman test, p < 0.05. Plant species: sugar beet and chard (Beta vulgaris subsp. vulgaris), Atriplex hortensis, Chenopodium album, Amaranthus retroflexus. Results detail: in males, sugar beet gave significant time (p = 0.016) and visits (p = 0.006) but first choice did not differ (chi2 = 6.22, p = 0.101); in females, Atriplex hortensis first choice was not significant (p = 0.343) and time p = 0.066; female Amaranthus retroflexus time was borderline (p = 0.049) while first choice (p = 0.164) and visits (p = 0.327) were not significant; no repellent response in either sex. Males on Atriplex hortensis: first choice 17 against 19 in the controls (chi2 = 11.33, p = 0.010), time Friedman chi2 = 11.09, df = 3, printed p < 0.001, visits chi2 = 19.22, p < 0.001; male Chenopodium album first choice 15 against 21 (chi2 = 6.89, p = 0.076). Whether excluded weevils were replaced, or weevils reused, is not stated. Leaf odour only, in the laboratory; no host-finding distance or field response.
quote: Males, but not females, responded positively to the leaf odour of the garden orache (A. hortensis), and no response was observed when the weevils were tested with the leaf odours of fat hen (C. album) or common amaranth (A. retroflexus).
